fieldworkDocument.title: Measgaichte / Miscellaneous
fieldworkDocument.note: [NOTES: note added on the first page – last 3 words on list by T. MacRae, North Lochs.]

item.description: not sure of English equivalent but this plant was boiled and taken for stomach complaints.
orphan.
to socialise, mix among other people.
late evening, just before it darkens.
hospitality, especially hospitality given to travellers delayed by bad weather conditions.
said when one had consumed a fair amount of strong drink. “Nach tu a ghabh a smoids deoch a raoir.”
looking at the darker side of things, e.g. “Tha i dol a shileadh a maireach Iain.” “Och eisd tha thusa làn de na marannan.”
a useless tonic. “Chan eil fhios agam dè an scumalaig gun fheum a bh’ann.”
tasteless.
a large hole in the strand filled with salt water.
in cahoots, e.g. “Bha iad ann an trochans ri chèile.”
a blow.
quietly, stealthily, e.g. “Chaidh mi sios dh’an rùm gu fàilidh.”
to creep up unexpectedly behind something and catch it unawares. This is used especially of catching a sheep but could also be applied to humans.
a foolish error or mistake. “Nach mise rinn a bhringlaid.”
a tall thin person.
a good catch. “Nach tu a rinn a sgaid a raoir aig an iasgach.”
a surprise find. “Nach tu a fhuair a foradh air a’ chladach an dè.”
where fresh water and salt water meet.
a small, chubby person.
applied to a harum-scarum young child.
same as above [i.e. mualainte (q.v.)]. Have also heard this word used in the context of a flighty woman.
a wreath.
fine ashes obtained from coal burning fire; finer than peat ashes.
black stripes appearing in cattle’s excrement. Taken as a sign of impending poor health and especially as a sign of constipation.
when animals were afflicted by ‘galair an domalais’ this was the term given to the bubble-like feature in their excrement.
blister or lump between the fingers.
a lazy fellow.
birch wood.
refers to the practice of milkmaids bringing milk daily from the shielings to the village below them.
a drink consisting of milk and water.
fresh milk drunk from the pail.
a large portion of scone given with butter and crowdie.

to decide, e.g. “Thug sinn mun aisidh an seòl a chuir rithe.” “Thug mi mun aisidh ceist neo dhà a chur air na fir.” “Thug e mun aisidh fear lagh fhaicinn.” [NOTES: ‘supplied by Torcuil MacRae, North Lochs, Lewis.’]
pointless. Would be said of pointless work. “’Se eideis obrach a bh’ann.” [NOTES: ‘supplied by Torcuil MacRae, North Lochs, Lewis.’]
group of men gathered together making a lot of noise. [NOTES: ‘supplied by Torcuil MacRae, North Lochs, Lewis.’]
The above three words were supplied by Torcuil MacRae, North Lochs, Lewis.
